scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Gumboot dance began in the late 1800s among black miners in South African gold mines near Johannesburg.
The miners, working in flooded, dark tunnels and forbidden to speak, used rhythmic stamping and slapping on their gumboots to communicate secretly.
This coded language evolved into a dance form that parodied mine guards and expressed miners' experiences.
on_screen: Map: South Africa · Africa

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a secret communication method in mines, Gumboot dance became a form of social resistance and cultural expression.
It parodies mine authorities and conveys miners' hardships and hopes.
Today it is performed at festivals, cultural events, and educational settings, symbolizing resilience and heritage.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Originally unaccompanied, Gumboot dance uses the boots and body as idiophones producing percussive rhythms.
Later, guitar, accordion, and violin were added in performances.
Listen for the Wellington boots with bells, body percussion, guitar, accordion.
The pulse is polyrhythmic, layered.

A layered texture of rhythmic boot stomps, hand slaps, and claps punctuated by bells and rattles, supported by melodic guitar and accordion lines, evoking the noisy mine environment and coded communication.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear rubber Wellington boots (gumboots), often embellished with bells or rattles around the ankles.
Boots may be painted or decorated.
Costumes can vary from casual work clothes to coordinated outfits, sometimes including school uniforms or protective helmets.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Groups like Black Umfolosi from Zimbabwe are known for Gumboot dance performances.
The Rishile Gumboot Dancers of Soweto have toured internationally.
While rooted in South African mines, Gumboot dance has spread to other African countries and global communities.
Gumboot dance descends from African traditional dances and idiophonic body percussion, adapted by miners under apartheid.
